claim: The archive holds 448 entries recording something student government put on.
entry_title: Count of every event carrying a "kind" field: concert 84, speaker 41, film 6, festival 18, tradition 39, service 89, program 130, other 41. Matches the figure site/events.html prints.

claim: 184 of those 448 fall in the ten academic years from 1970-71 to 1979-80.
entry_title: Count of kind-carrying events in years 1970-71 through 1979-80. Matches the "1970s 184" filter on site/events.html.

claim: The lecture series brought James Farmer in March 1969, which the Herald called a first for the series.
entry_title: James Farmer speaks, a first for the lecture series

claim: Dick Gregory spoke on the series in the autumn of 1970.
entry_title: Dick Gregory speaks after a second test of the new speaker policy

claim: Julian Bond spoke in December 1970.
entry_title: Julian Bond speaks on a Sunday

claim: Bernadette Devlin spoke in February 1971.
entry_title: Bernadette Devlin speaks on a Friday night

claim: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan were sponsored jointly with the University Lecture Series.
entry_title: Coretta Scott King and Betty Friedan speak on the joint lecture series

claim: Buckminster Fuller was sponsored jointly with the University Lecture Series.
entry_title: Buckminster Fuller lectures on 'Humans in the Universe'

claim: Senator Edmund Muskie used an ASG lecture on 11 December 1973 to call for Nixon's impeachment.
entry_title: Edmund Muskie calls for Nixon's impeachment in an ASG lecture

claim: Thirty-four of the 41 lecture entries in the archive are dated before July 1979.
entry_title: Count of events with kind "speaker": 41 in total, 34 dated on or before 1979-06-30. The remaining seven are 1993-10-12 (two), 2015-09-15, 2017-02-14, 2018-02-28, 2018-03-19 and 2023-04-11.

claim: Ike and Tina Turner played Homecoming 1971 before an estimated 12,000.
entry_title: Ike and Tina Turner headline Homecoming before about 12,000

claim: Chicago played a free concert in October 1972.
entry_title: Chicago plays a free concert

claim: Jethro Tull followed three weeks later; the 1973 Talisman recorded that many in the audience called it the best concert ever staged at Western, and that it was a major financial loss.
entry_title: Jethro Tull sells tickets and loses money

claim: Kiss played Van Meter in December 1974 with fire-eating and stage blood, after which Ron Beck, who did the booking, said he would never again help book the genre because it had no educational value for students.
entry_title: Kiss plays Van Meter and Ron Beck swears off the genre

claim: Ron Beck was the person doing the concert booking.
entry_title: Protest produces a coalition for change in concert booking

claim: The Regents added $11,000 to the ASG allotment in August 1973.
entry_title: An $11,000 budget increase pays for the concert and lecture year

claim: The Regents added $16,000 to the entertainment budget in August 1975, which president Steve Henry said bought a second free concert.
entry_title: Regents add $16,000 to the entertainment budget and buy a second free concert

claim: ASG ran on $42,000 for entertainment in 1974-75.
entry_title: A $42,000 entertainment budget, $27,000 of it for two free concerts

claim: Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins lost $13,200 in November 1977.
entry_title: Dave Mason and Kenny Loggins lose $13,200

claim: Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick lost about $12,000 on Valentine's Day 1978.
entry_title: Atlanta Rhythm Section and Brick lose $12,000 on Valentine's Day

claim: The Spinners and Wet Willie played free to 7,500 in January 1976.
entry_title: The Spinners and Wet Willie drew 7,500 to a free concert

claim: Barry Manilow played free to 7,000 in November 1976.
entry_title: Barry Manilow plays free to 7,000 and cuts his set short

claim: Chicago drew 10,450 on 15 October 1976 and grossed $53,092 against a $25,000 fee.
entry_title: Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert

claim: The 1977 Talisman called Chicago Western's most financially successful concert (attributed, not asserted).
entry_title: Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert

claim: About thirty students picketed the doors of the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert in October 1974.
entry_title: Students picket the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert

claim: Within days the Herald reported a coalition seeking change in the booking; the committee that came out of it wanted the activities vice president to negotiate with acts, and settled for an advisory role because Kentucky law barred a student from controlling the funds.
entry_title: Protest produces a coalition for change in concert booking

claim: ASG's Student Activities Committee was in operation from 2 December 1975, with seventeen members chosen from 63 applicants, seven for concerts, five for lectures and five for publicity.
entry_title: ASG creates a student activities committee for concerts, lectures and publicity

claim: The committee was set up after a semester of argument over who should decide what came to campus, and 17 of 63 applicants were chosen.
entry_title: ASG sets up a Student Activities Committee to choose the acts

claim: ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts in 1977-78; dean of student affairs Charles Keown asked the Board of Regents to halve its entertainment budget and to study whether the University Center Board should take the programming over; Bob Moore argued on 29 April 1978 that students would have less involvement; the Regents let ASG keep the full $62,000 and directed President Downing to appoint the study committee.
entry_title: $23,000 of losses nearly cost ASG the concert programme

claim: ASG hired the work out to Sunshine Promotions of Indianapolis for 13 per cent of net profits.
entry_title: ASG hands its concerts to an outside promoter

claim: Eight days before the Homecoming show the firm had still not signed, because it would not post the $100,000 performance bond Western required.
entry_title: ASG's promoter had not signed a contract days before the Player and Exile concert

claim: Player and Exile grossed $25,694.29 after tax against $24,000 of production costs.
entry_title: Player and Exile play the Homecoming concert

claim: The Herald told ASG on 9 November 1978 to get out of the concert business.
entry_title: The Herald tells ASG to quit the concert business

claim: The Outlaws cancelled in December 1978 after 242 tickets sold.
entry_title: The Outlaws cancel after 242 tickets sell

claim: On 31 March 1979 the Board of Regents approved a rebuilt University Center Board and gave it $80,000 for programming; from the autumn its committees of students and administrators ran the lectures and concerts ASG had been running; ASG kept three seats on a board that also held the Interfraternity and Panhellenic councils, United Black Students, the two residence hall councils, two other students and three faculty members; programs coordinator Tim Nemeth said it would involve more student participation and then put its maximum at ten students against the fifty involved under ASG.
entry_title: The Regents take concerts and lectures away from ASG

claim: President Jamie Hargrove said the transfer cost ASG between $60,000 and $70,000 of budget and no real power, and the year that followed was spent on opinion polls and a radio phone-in.
entry_title: ASG replaces concerts with opinion polls and a radio phone-in

claim: Eighty of the archive's 84 concert entries are dated before 31 March 1979.
entry_title: Count of events with kind "concert": 84 in total, 80 dated before 1979-03-31. Matches the note printed at the head of the Concerts section of site/events.html.

claim: Of the four concert-tagged entries after that date, three are from 1999: Amanda Coates campaigned on bringing a major act to the Hill.
entry_title: A candidate promises the Dave Matthews Band

claim: Coates was still pursuing a concert in August 1999.
entry_title: Coates's quest for a concert continues

claim: An October 1999 Herald headline said big-name concerts might arrive; the paper trail stops at the possibility.
entry_title: "Big-Name Concerts May Arrive on Campus"

claim: The fourth is a senate resolution of 2011 endorsing a benefit concert run by two other student groups.
entry_title: Senate endorsed the Topper Talent Benefit Concert and funded One Planet Day

claim: Four presidents have left before their year was out.
entry_title: Marcel Bush (1981-82), Nick Todd (2004-05), Robert Watkins (2006-07), Johnathon Boles (2008-09); the four handovers listed on site/irregular.html.

claim: Marcel Bush resigned on 14 January 1982.
entry_title: ASG president Marcel Bush resigns

claim: David Payne was Bush's administrative vice president and took the balance of the term.
entry_title: leader: Marcel Bush (note) - SGA's 2001 roster of former presidents records that he resigned in January 1982 and that administrative vice president David Payne filled the position

claim: The Board of Regents minutes of 30 January 1982 name Payne the president.
entry_title: Board of Regents minutes name David Payne the new SGA president

claim: The Board seat did not travel with the office; it went instead to a campus-wide special election in February 1982.
entry_title: leader: Marcel Bush (note) - "The roster stars Bush as a student regent and does not star Payne, which is why the Board seat went to a special election in February 1982 rather than passing with the presidency." Five students filed: see the entry "Five students seek the student regent seat".

claim: Sandra Norfleet won the seat on a runoff.
entry_title: Sandra Norfleet elected student regent

claim: The Herald measured Norfleet's term at two months.
entry_title: Norfleet's short regent term nears its end

claim: Nick Todd resigned in July 2004 after an investigation into an SGA Dining Dollars account, and his executive vice president Katie Dawson acted as president through the summer until the special election of 14 and 15 September.
entry_title: SGA president Nick Todd resigned amid funds investigation

claim: No source found records Katie Dawson being sworn in.
entry_title: leader: Katie Dawson (note) - "No source found says she was sworn in... described her only as acting president, which is how this site records her."

claim: Patti Johnson was the only student to come forward for the September 2004 special election.
entry_title: Patti Johnson emerged as the only candidate in the special election

claim: Three people held the presidency within twelve months in 2004-05.
entry_title: Nick Todd, Katie Dawson and Patti Johnson are all recorded as holding the office in 2004-05; see the three leader records for that year and the 2004-05 panel on site/irregular.html.

claim: SGA's senate minutes for 28 November 2006 record Rob Watkins's resignation being read to the chamber, with senators told Jeanne Johnson would be sworn in at the Winter Banquet a week later.
entry_title: Watkins resigned as SGA president and student regent

claim: The minutes of 5 December 2006 list the executive vice presidency as vacant because Johnson had moved up.
entry_title: Senate tabled two resolutions for lack of quorum at Winter Banquet meeting

claim: The Board seat did not move with the presidency and Johnson had to win it in a February 2007 special election.
entry_title: Johnson won the student regent election; SGA seated a full senate

claim: Kayla Shelton succeeded Johnathon Boles as president but not as regent, the seat stood empty 26 days, and Reagan Gilley won a special election 477 to 224.
entry_title: Reagan Gilley won the special student regent election

claim: The plaque in the SGA Chambers gives one name to a year; no plate carries Nick Todd's name.
entry_title: leader: Nick Todd (note) - "No plate on the Chambers wall carries his name; the 2004-05 plate reads Patti Johnson."

claim: No plate carries Reagan Gilley's name.
entry_title: leader: Reagan Gilley - "missing_from_plaque": true; also listed under "No plate on the wall" on site/irregular.html

claim: Katie Dawson is plated only for 2005-06.
entry_title: leader: Katie Dawson (note) - "She is on the Chambers wall for 2005-06 only, so the plaque does not record this stretch."

claim: Jeanne Johnson is plated only for 2007-08, the full term she won in her own right.
entry_title: leader: Jeanne Johnson (note) - "The Chambers wall carries her only for 2007-08, the full term she was elected to in her own right."

claim: The earliest standing service in the record is a calendar of the month's events posted outside the Associated Students office in January 1967.
entry_title: A monthly events calendar posted outside the Associated Students office

claim: In May 1967 the Herald argued Western should run a student book exchange as Murray State and the University of Louisville did, and the exchange on this campus belonged to the Veterans Club.
entry_title: The case for a student book exchange

claim: ASG ran a book exchange at the start of term in September 1969.
entry_title: A book exchange runs at the start of term

claim: ASG announced another book exchange in December 1972.
entry_title: ASG announces a book exchange

claim: By January 1976 ASG was running the exchange with Veterans on Campus, selling more than 600 books at 25 cents profit each.
entry_title: ASG and Veterans on Campus run a book exchange against the bookstore

claim: The exchange sold more than 1,100 books by February 1977.
entry_title: Book exchange sells more than 1,100 books

claim: The swap was called off for the spring of 1978.
entry_title: The book swap is called off for the spring

claim: ASG voted to study a book exchange in September 1984.
entry_title: ASG votes to study a book exchange

claim: Over the Christmas break four people keyed the listings into an IBM Personal Computer; the Book Exchanger appeared as a tabloid in the first week of the spring semester; senior class president Danny Broderick said ASG made no money from it and called it "a labor of love."
entry_title: The book exchanger's first edition

claim: By November 1987 the Book Exchanger had raised about $60 the previous autumn against printing costs of about $653, and the student affairs chairman said he would recommend dropping it if that run failed.
entry_title: The Book Exchanger gets a third semester and a warning

claim: Twenty-one Bowling Green merchants signed the discount programme in December 1969.
entry_title: Twenty-one merchants sign the discount programme

claim: The discount card covered 29 merchants by May 1977.
entry_title: Student discount card covers 29 merchants

claim: In September 1981 ASG filed complaints against a Texas and Georgia firm that had taken $275 from each of at least four Bowling Green merchants for ASG-endorsed cards that were never produced.
entry_title: The discount cards that never existed

claim: Marcel Bush spent three weeks chasing the printer and found a disconnected number, an Atlanta number nobody answered and a returned letter.
entry_title: 14,000 cards, a dead phone line and a returned letter

claim: In November 1983 ASG printed its own card after an agreement with a Missouri company collapsed, putting nine businesses on it, seven of which had paid that company and never got a refund; president Jack Smith said of them, "They got what they paid for."
entry_title: ASG prints the discount card itself

claim: ASG took production in house in August 1986, after a later printer was indicted over the $500 he owed it.
entry_title: ASG takes over the student discount card

claim: A volunteer escort service began in September 1982, run with Interhall Council and the university police, walking women anywhere on campus from dark until midnight on a single telephone number; its coordinator said it had filled 500 to 600 requests in its first year, and the public safety director said requests had tripled after two rapes the previous year.
entry_title: A volunteer student escort service

claim: When Provide-A-Ride's contract lapsed in September 2009, three students set up a taxi charging $5 a rider.
entry_title: Provide-A-Ride was suspended and students started their own taxi

claim: The service's 2010 report counted more than 9,200 passengers in 2009-10, with none for 2008-09 because a fire had destroyed the handwritten logs.
entry_title: Provide-A-Ride carried more than 9,200 passengers in a year

claim: $1,225 for 175 transcript vouchers in 2012.
entry_title: Senate funds a transcript voucher programme

claim: $800 for 80 replacement student ID vouchers in 2013.
entry_title: ID voucher programme halved the cost of a replacement card

claim: $500 for 25 counselling registration vouchers in 2018.
entry_title: Counselling voucher programme covered the registration fee

claim: $500 for 20 dental cleanings in 2022.
entry_title: Free teeth cleanings through the dental hygiene programme
